title: Worldly wisdom and the wisdom of God
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ εἰκὸς τὰ γεγραμμένα ἐν τῇ πρὸς Κορινθίους προτέρᾳ τῷ Παύλῳ, ὡς πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ μέγα φυσῶντας ἐπὶ τῇ Ἑλληνικῇ σοφίᾳ, κεκινηκέναι τινὰς, ὡς τοῦ λόγου μὴ βουλομένου σοφούς. ἀλλ᾿ ἀκουέτω ὁ τὰ τοιαῦτα νομίζων ὅτι. ὥσπερ διαβάλλων ἀνθρώπους φαύλους ὁ λόγος φησὶν αὐτοὺς εἶναι οὐ περὶ τῶν νοητῶν καὶ ἀοράτων καὶ αἰωνίων σοφοὺς, ἀλλὰ περὶ μόνων τῶν αἰσθητῶν πραγματευσαμένους καὶ ἐν τούτοις τὰ πάντα τιθεμένους εἶναι σοφοὺς τοῦ κόσμου· οὕτως καὶ πολλῶν ὄντων δογμάτων. τὰ μὲν συναγορεύοντα ὕλῃ καὶ σώμασι καὶ πάντα φάσκοντα εἶναι σώματα τὰ προηγουμένως ὑφεστηκότα καὶ μηδὲν παρὰ ταῦτα εἶναι ἄλλο, εἴτε λεγόμενον ἀόρατον εἴτ᾿ ὀνομαζόμενον ἀσώματον. φησὶν εἶναι „σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου“ καταργουμένην καὶ μωραινομένην καὶ σοφίαν τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου· τὰ δὲ μετατιθέντα τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν τῇδε πραγμάτων ἐπὶ τὴν παρὰ θεῷ μακαριότητα καὶ τὴν καλουμένην αὐτοῦ βασιλείαν. καὶ διδάσκοντα καταφρονεῖν μὲν ὡς προσκαίρων πάντων τῶν αἰσθητῶν καὶ βλεπομένων σπεύδειν δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ ἀόρατα καὶ σκοπεῖν τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα, ταῦτά φησι „σοφίαν“ εἶναι „θεοῦ“. φιλαλήθης δ᾿ ὢν ὁ Παῦλός φησι περί τινων ἐν Ἕλλησι σοφῶν, ἐν οἷς ἀληθεύουσιν. „ὅτι γνόντες τὸν θεὸν οὐχ ὡς θεὸν ἐδόξασαν ἢ ηὐχαρίστησαν.“ καὶ μαρτυρεῖ αὐτοῖς ἐγνωκέναι θεόν· λέγει δὲ καὶ τοῦτ᾿ οὐκ ἀθεεὶ αὐτοῖς γεγονέναι ἐν οἷς γράφει τὸ „ὁ θεὸς γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἐφανέρωσεν.“ αἰνισσόμενος οἶμαι τοὺς ἀναβαίνοντας ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρατῶν ἐπὶ τὰ νοητὰ, ὅτε γράφει ὅτι „τὰ ἀόρατα τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται. ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους, διότι γνόντες τὸν θεὸν οὐχ ὡς θεὸν ἐδόξασαν ἢ ηὐχαρίστησαν.“
pass_a_gloss: But [it is] likely (εἰκός) that the things written by Paul in the first [letter] to the Corinthians, as to Greeks and [people] puffing up greatly (μέγα φυσάω) over the Greek wisdom, moved (κινέω) some, as though the word did not wish [people to be] wise. But let the one thinking such things hear that, just as the word, slandering/censuring (διαβάλλω) worthless (φαῦλοι) men, says them to be not wise about the intelligible (νοητά) and invisible (ἀόρατα) and eternal (αἰώνια) [things], but, having busied themselves (πραγματεύομαι) about the sensible (αἰσθητά) only and placing (τίθημι) all things in these, to be wise of the world (κόσμος); so also, there being many doctrines (δόγματα), those speaking in support of (συναγορεύω) matter (ὕλη) and bodies (σώματα) and asserting (φάσκω) that all the things subsisting primarily (προηγουμένως ὑφίσταμαι) are bodies and nothing else is beside these, whether called invisible or named incorporeal (ἀσώματον), it says are ‘wisdom of the world’ being made of no effect (καταργέω) and made foolish (μωραίνω) and wisdom of this age (αἰών); but those transferring (μετατίθημι) the soul (ψυχή) from the affairs here (τῇδε) to the blessedness (μακαριότης) with God and his so-called kingdom (βασιλεία), and teaching to despise (καταφρονέω) as temporary (πρόσκαιρα) all the sensible and seen (βλεπόμενα) [things], and to hasten (σπεύδω) toward the invisible and look at (σκοπέω) the not-seen, these it says are ‘wisdom’ ‘of God.’ And being a truth-lover (φιλαλήθης) Paul says about certain wise among Greeks, in [the points] in which they speak truth (ἀληθεύω), ‘that having known (γινώσκω) God they did not glorify (δοξάζω) [him] as God or give thanks (εὐχαριστέω).’ And he testifies to them to have known God; and he says also this to have happened to them not without God (οὐκ ἀθεεί), in which he writes ‘for God manifested (φανερόω) [it] to them,’ hinting (αἰνίσσομαι), I think, at those ascending (ἀναβαίνω) from the visible (ὁρατά) to the intelligible, when he writes that ‘the invisible [things] of God from creation (κτίσις) of world by the things made (ποιήματα) being understood (νοέω) are clearly seen (καθοράω), both his everlasting (ἀΐδιος) power (δύναμις) and divinity (θειότης), so that they are without excuse (ἀναπολόγητοι), because having known God they did not glorify [him] as God or give thanks.’
pass_b_english: But it is likely that what Paul wrote in the First Letter to the Corinthians, addressed as it was to Greeks who were greatly puffed up over Greek wisdom, has moved some to think that our teaching does not want wise men. Let anyone who thinks so hear this. When the word censures worthless men, it says that they are not wise about things intelligible, invisible and eternal, but that, having busied themselves with the things of sense alone and placing everything in these, they are wise men of the world. In the same way, since there are many doctrines, it says that those which plead for matter and bodies, and assert that all things that primarily exist are bodies and that there is nothing else besides them, whether called invisible or named incorporeal, are “the wisdom of the world,” which is brought to nothing and made foolish, and the wisdom of this age (1 Corinthians 1:20; 2:6). But those which carry the soul over from the affairs of this world to the blessedness that is with God and to what is called his kingdom, and which teach people to despise all things perceived by sense and seen, as being temporary, and to hasten toward things invisible and to look at the things that are not seen (2 Corinthians 4:18), these it says are “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 2:7).

Paul, as a lover of truth, says of certain wise men among the Greeks, in the points where they speak truly, “that, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:21). He bears witness that they had known God; and he says too that this did not come to them without God, where he writes: “for God has shown it to them” (Romans 1:19). He is hinting, I think, at those who ascend from things visible to things intelligible, when he writes that “the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:20–21).

choices.choice: ὁ λόγος in this chapter means the word of Scripture (here Paul's letters) and is rendered ‘the word’ in lowercase, and ‘our teaching’ in the first sentence (τοῦ λόγου μὴ βουλομένου σοφούς). ‘wise men of the world’ (σοφοὺς τοῦ κόσμου) in the first comparison is left unquoted because the Greek does not mark it as a quotation. ‘the wisdom of the world, which is brought to nothing and made foolish, and the wisdom of this age’ combines 1 Corinthians 1:20 (ἐμώρανεν ὁ θεὸς τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου) and 2:6 (σοφίαν … τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου … τῶν καταργουμένων); compare also 1 Corinthians 3:19. ‘to look at the things that are not seen … temporary’ alludes to 2 Corinthians 4:18 (σκοπούντων … τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα· τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα). ‘the wisdom of God’ cited as 1 Corinthians 2:7 (θεοῦ σοφίαν); the phrase also occurs at 1:21 and 1:24. Romans 1:19–21 is quoted in Origen's order: verse 21 first, then 19, then 20–21. ἀΐδιος rendered ‘eternal’ (as in common English versions of Romans 1:20). ‘his kingdom’ (τὴν καλουμένην αὐτοῦ βασιλείαν) is the kingdom of God; the pronoun stays lowercase. ‘Greek’ (Ἑλληνική) wisdom: Origen means pagan philosophical culture.
Fixed the garbled first comparison: ‘it says that they are not wise about things intelligible … but that … they are wise men of the world’ (οὐ … σοφούς, ἀλλὰ … εἶναι σοφοὺς τοῦ κόσμου)
‘teach us to despise’ changed to ‘teach people to despise’ (Greek has no ‘us’)
Checked 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6, 2:7, 2 Corinthians 4:18, Romans 1:19–21; no other change
